case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal employee–reservist activated to active duty under 10 U.S.C. § 12301(d) during an ongoing national emergency is entitled to Reservist Differential Pay because that service counts as being “called or ordered to active duty under” a qualifying “provision of law … during a national emergency.”
case_analysis.legal_provision: Primary: 5 U.S.C. § 5538 (Reservist Differential Pay); Incorporated definition: 10 U.S.C. § 101(a)(13)(B) (definition of “contingency operation” referencing service “during a national emergency”); Activation authority at issue: 10 U.S.C. § 12301(d).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues the Federal Circuit adopted an atextual rule by effectively excluding voluntary activations under § 12301(d) from differential pay even when they occur during a national emergency (and even when orders expressly invoke an emergency declaration). On petitioner’s reading, § 5538’s entitlement turns on whether the reservist was ordered to duty under a statutory authority listed/covered by the incorporated “contingency operation” definition and the service occurred “during a national emergency,” not on whether the emergency declaration was the specific legal trigger for the orders. Thus, activation under § 12301(d) during a declared national emergency should qualify, and the court below misread the statute by requiring a tighter causal nexus between the emergency declaration and the orders.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent maintains petitioner is not entitled to differential pay because § 5538 eligibility is limited to reservists serving in a qualifying “contingency operation” as defined by § 101(a)(13), and service under § 12301(d) does not automatically qualify merely because a national emergency exists. The government also argues the case is a poor vehicle: petitioner did not properly raise certain fact-specific arguments in the Federal Circuit (e.g., whether the express emergency invocation in his orders is sufficient), the decision below is nonprecedential and did not resolve that question, and petitioner never submitted the required request/documentation to the agency to calculate differential pay. Respondent invokes waiver/vehicle principles (“not pressed or passed upon”) and emphasizes administrative prerequisites for payment calculations.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s textual argument that “during a national emergency” in § 101(a)(13)(B) is ordinarily temporal is the strongest merits point, and I do not discount it. But as Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Gorsuch stress, petitioner’s current theory—especially that an express emergency reference in his particular § 12301(d) orders supplies the statutory link—was not “pressed or passed upon” below, and United States v. Williams counsels against our deciding that predicate in the first instance. The administrative-record gaps and the apparent failure to complete the agency’s documentation/request process further make a broad merits ruling look advisory and institutionally imprudent. Consistent with judicial minimalism, I would affirm for Respondent on preservation/vehicle grounds and leave the merits question for a case that squarely presents it on a developed record.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s vehicle argument under United States v. Williams is the strongest counter, and I accept that we generally avoid deciding questions not “pressed or passed upon” below. But Williams is a prudential restraint, not a license to affirm on an atextual narrowing construction of § 101(a)(13)(B)’s residual clause; the statutory text (“any other provision of law during…a national emergency”) is temporal, and Justice Alito’s and Justice Kagan’s efforts to require an emergency-linked causal nexus rewrite “during” into “because of.” The record-development and agency-process issues identified by the Chief Justice and Justice Gorsuch go to proof and calculation, not to the legal meaning of the cross-reference Congress enacted. Absent a true jurisdictional defect, I would adhere to the ordinary meaning and remand for proper application on a developed record rather than affirm based on preservation concerns that effectively decide the merits against the statute’s text.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s textual point that “during” in § 101(a)(13)(B) is ordinarily temporal is the best merits argument for petitioner, and I do not dispute that the clause, in isolation, can be read broadly. But as Justice Kagan emphasizes, § 5538 is triggered only when the employee is “called or ordered to active duty under” a qualifying contingency-operation framework, and it is not clear that voluntary § 12301(d) service becomes “under” a qualifying provision simply because a standing national emergency exists—especially given Congress’s carefully enumerated structure. Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Gorsuch’s United States v. Williams vehicle point reinforces that this case is a poor posture to decide the fact-bound theory about whether petitioner’s particular orders (or the agency documentation process) supply the necessary statutory link, and we should not issue an effectively advisory ruling detached from the administrative mechanism for computing differential pay. None of the petitioner-side responses—particularly Justice Sotomayor’s fairness-and-purpose framing—overcomes those preservation and statutory-structure concerns under a textualist, context-sensitive approach.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s United States v. Williams vehicle point is serious, but Williams is a prudential practice about questions not pressed or passed upon—not a mandate to deny relief when the statutory interpretive issue (the meaning of “during a national emergency” as incorporated into § 5538) is the very basis of the lower court’s judgment and the parties’ dispute. Even if there are factual gaps about the content of particular orders or the agency’s documentation steps, those go to proof and computation, not to the threshold eligibility question that the Federal Circuit necessarily resolved in adopting a narrowing construction. On the merits, Justice Kagan’s administrability worry about long-running emergencies cannot justify rewriting “during” into “because of,” especially in a remedial pay-protection statute aimed at preventing concrete harm to service members and their families. The better course is to reject the atextual causal-nexus limitation and remand for application and record development rather than affirm on a vehicle theory that would leave an erroneous merits rule in place.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right that “during” most naturally carries a temporal meaning, and I am not persuaded by any invitation to read “during” as “because of.” But that textual point does not answer the separate structural problem: § 5538 turns on being “called or ordered to active duty under” a provision “referred to in” § 101(a)(13)(B), and reading the residual clause to convert any activation authority (including § 12301(d)) into qualifying service whenever any national emergency exists would largely nullify Congress’s enumerated list and make the benefit track the duration of often long-running emergencies without clearer instruction. Chief Justice Roberts’s Williams vehicle point strengthens my reluctance to decide the petitioner’s order-specific “express emergency invocation” theory in the first instance, especially given the record/administrative-process gaps that Justice Barrett and Justice Kavanaugh highlight. On pragmatic textualist grounds—text in context plus administrability—I would affirm/deny relief on this record without announcing the broad eligibility rule petitioner seeks.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right that “during a national emergency” is most naturally temporal, and I share his skepticism of judicially importing a causal nexus not found in the text. But Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on United States v. Williams is dispositive for me here: the Federal Circuit did not “press or pass upon” the petitioner’s order-specific theory (including any express emergency invocation), and we should not decide that predicate question in the first instance. Add the administrative-record gaps (noted by the Chief and Justice Kagan) concerning the agency’s required request/documentation process, and a merits ruling risks becoming advisory and unmoored from an actual entitlement determination. On this vehicle, I would affirm for Respondent while leaving the statutory-meaning question for a case that cleanly presents it.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point—that “during a national emergency” in § 101(a)(13)(B) is naturally temporal and not causal—has real force on the merits, and I agree we should be wary of reading extra limitations into a statute. But Chief Justice Roberts’s vehicle argument under United States v. Williams is dispositive for me here: the Federal Circuit did not press or pass upon petitioner’s theory that an express emergency reference in his particular § 12301(d) orders supplies the needed statutory link, and I am not willing to decide that fact-bound predicate in the first instance. Justice Sotomayor is right that Williams is prudential, not jurisdictional, but prudence is exactly what institutional restraint requires when the administrative record is incomplete and petitioner appears not to have complied with the agency’s documentation/request process needed to compute any differential pay—otherwise we risk an advisory merits pronouncement untethered to a workable remedy. On this record, I would deny relief/affirm without resolving the broader interpretive dispute about § 5538’s incorporation of § 101(a)(13)(B).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right that “during” in § 101(a)(13)(B) ordinarily carries a temporal meaning, and I do not rest my view on importing an atextual “because of” requirement. But even on a purely temporal reading, the operative trigger in § 5538—being “called or ordered to active duty under” a provision “referred to in” § 101(a)(13)(B)—is not satisfied merely by pointing to a standing national emergency when the underlying call-up authority is § 12301(d), unless the necessary statutory linkage and factual predicates are established. Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Gorsuch’s Williams point matters here: the “orders expressly invoking an emergency” theory and the administratively relevant prerequisites for calculating differential pay were not pressed or passed upon below, and deciding them now would risk an advisory, record-free pronouncement. In this posture, I would affirm/deny relief on vehicle and preservation grounds without broadening § 5538 to cover § 12301(d) absent developed findings about the orders and process.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Sotomayor persuasively press the textual point that “during a national emergency” in § 101(a)(13)(B) can read temporally rather than causally, and I do not dismiss that merits argument. But Chief Justice Roberts’s United States v. Williams preservation/vehicle concern remains dispositive for me: petitioner’s current theory that the express emergency reference in his particular § 12301(d) orders supplies the statutory link was not “pressed or passed upon” below, and deciding it now would require us to resolve fact- and record-dependent predicates in the first instance. Justice Kagan’s administrability/record point reinforces the institutional problem: with apparent gaps in the agency-request/documentation process needed to compute any differential pay, a broad merits ruling risks being untethered to an actually administrable entitlement determination. On progressive-pragmatist and procedural-fairness grounds, I would affirm/deny relief on this record without foreclosing the statutory question in a cleaner case.

John Roberts.reasoning: Even assuming 5 U.S.C. § 5538 could encompass some activations under 10 U.S.C. § 12301(d) during a declared national emergency via the incorporated definition in 10 U.S.C. § 101(a)(13)(B), this case is a poor vehicle because key factual/legal predicates were not developed or resolved below. The Federal Circuit’s nonprecedential decision did not decide whether an express invocation of an emergency declaration in orders suffices, and this Court ordinarily declines review of issues “not pressed or passed upon” in the court of appeals. United States v. Williams, 504 U.S. 36, 41 (1992). In addition, petitioner’s failure to pursue the agency’s required documentation/request process for calculating differential pay underscores that a narrow, institution-preserving disposition is to deny relief here without announcing a broad rule about § 12301(d).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Applying textualism, 5 U.S.C. § 5538 ties entitlement to whether the employee was “called or ordered to active duty under” a provision of law incorporated through 10 U.S.C. § 101(a)(13)(B), which includes “any other provision of law during … a national emergency declared by the President or Congress.” The ordinary public meaning of “during” is temporal, not causal, so the statute requires overlap with a declared national emergency, not that the emergency declaration be the legal trigger for the orders; adding a causal-nexus requirement rewrites the text. Activation under 10 U.S.C. § 12301(d) is a “provision of law,” and if the service occurred during a declared national emergency, it fits § 101(a)(13)(B)’s residual clause as incorporated by § 5538. Consistent with United States v. Williams, 504 U.S. 36 (1992), the Court should enforce the cross-referenced statutory conditions as written rather than engrafting extra limitations absent from the text.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 5538 ties Reservist Differential Pay to service “called or ordered to active duty under” a qualifying contingency-operation framework, and 10 U.S.C. § 101(a)(13)(B) does not make § 12301(d) voluntary activations automatically qualifying merely because a national emergency is ongoing. The government’s vehicle objections are substantial: petitioner’s theory about whether an express emergency invocation in his orders suffices was not developed or resolved below, and this Court generally declines to decide questions “not pressed or passed upon.” United States v. Williams, 504 U.S. 36, 41 (1992). Practical consequences also counsel restraint where the claim appears to bypass established agency procedures requiring submission of orders and pay records to calculate any differential under § 5538.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The text of 10 U.S.C. § 101(a)(13)(B), incorporated through 5 U.S.C. § 5538, focuses on whether the reservist was “called or ordered to active duty under” a provision of law and served “during a national emergency,” not on whether the emergency declaration was the but-for legal trigger for the orders. An activation under 10 U.S.C. § 12301(d) is still an order “under” that statutory authority, and when it occurs during an ongoing declared national emergency—especially where the orders expressly invoke the emergency—it fits the statute’s ordinary meaning and remedial purpose of protecting reservists from pay loss. Limiting eligibility by adding an extra causal-nexus requirement risks arbitrarily denying differential pay to servicemembers and their families in circumstances Congress meant to cover, undermining fairness and access to benefits for those who serve. While vehicle/waiver concerns may matter at the cert stage, United States v. Williams, 504 U.S. 36 (1992), does not justify rewriting the statutory entitlement where the legal question is preserved and the statutory language is best read to include these orders.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 5538 ties entitlement to being “called or ordered to active duty under” a “provision of law referred to in” 10 U.S.C. § 101(a)(13)(B), and § 12301(d) is not among the enumerated qualifying provisions; treating the catchall phrase (“any other provision of law during … a national emergency”) as sweeping in § 12301(d) risks reading the statute to cover essentially any voluntary activation whenever an emergency is on the books, a result Congress did not clearly prescribe. Even if “during” in § 101(a)(13)(B) is most naturally temporal, the operative trigger in § 5538 is the activation authority “under” which the employee is ordered, and the Federal Circuit’s narrower approach is a workable, administrable line that avoids turning a limited pay differential into a broad, emergency-duration benefit. Moreover, the government’s vehicle points (arguments not pressed or passed upon, and administrative prerequisites for calculating differential pay) counsel against reversing on the merits in this posture. Consistent with United States v. Williams, 504 U.S. 36 (1992), the Court should resist expanding pay entitlements beyond the clear statutory conditions Congress set.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Even assuming ambiguity in how 5 U.S.C. § 5538 incorporates the 10 U.S.C. § 101(a)(13)(B) “during a national emergency” language, this petition is an improper vehicle: the arguments about whether petitioner’s particular orders expressly invoking an emergency declaration suffice were “not pressed or passed upon” below, and we generally do not decide such questions in the first instance. United States v. Williams, 504 U.S. 36, 41 (1992). In addition, petitioner’s apparent failure to pursue the agency’s required request/documentation for calculating differential pay underscores that any entitlement determination here would be advisory and premature. Given those threshold barriers, I would deny relief and vote for the Respondent without reaching a broader reading of § 5538’s merits.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Even assuming there is some statutory ambiguity in how 5 U.S.C. § 5538 incorporates the 10 U.S.C. § 101(a)(13) “contingency operation” definition for service “during a national emergency,” this case presents substantial vehicle problems that counsel restraint. Under United States v. Williams, 504 U.S. 36, 41 (1992), the Court generally declines to decide questions that were “not pressed or passed upon” below; here, the Federal Circuit’s nonprecedential decision did not resolve whether an express emergency invocation in orders under 10 U.S.C. § 12301(d) suffices, and petitioner did not properly develop that fact-specific theory. In addition, the record reflects petitioner did not complete the agency’s required request/documentation process necessary to calculate any differential pay, making the dispute practically unworkable as a clean merits vehicle. Given those institutional and procedural defects, I would vote to affirm/deny relief to petitioner on this record.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Textually, 5 U.S.C. § 5538 ties eligibility to active-duty service “under” a provision of law “referred to in” 10 U.S.C. § 101(a)(13)(B), and § 101(a)(13)(B) does not naturally read to sweep in all service merely because it occurs while a national emergency exists; its cross-references and structure suggest a more specific linkage to the emergency-related authorities Congress enumerated. Reading “during a national emergency” as purely temporal would risk collapsing the definition of “contingency operation” into virtually any activation in an era of standing emergency declarations, undermining the careful statutory list. In addition, even if petitioner’s orders’ reference to an emergency declaration could matter, that argument was not pressed or passed upon below, and this case presents vehicle problems (including unmet administrative prerequisites) that counsel against relief here under our ordinary waiver/vehicle principles. See United States v. Williams, 504 U.S. 36, 41 (1992).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Even assuming 5 U.S.C. § 5538 could plausibly be read to cover some service under 10 U.S.C. § 12301(d) when performed “during a national emergency” (via 10 U.S.C. § 101(a)(13)(B)), this case is an unsuitable vehicle because petitioner’s key theory—whether the express emergency invocation in his orders supplies the necessary statutory connection—was “not pressed or passed upon” in the Federal Circuit. Under United States v. Williams, 504 U.S. 36, 41 (1992), we generally decline to decide issues not properly raised and resolved below, and the nonprecedential, fact-bound decision here underscores that the lower court did not settle the broader legal question petitioner presents. Procedural fairness and practical consequences also counsel against review where petitioner did not complete the agency’s prerequisites for calculating and awarding differential pay (submission/request and documentation), risking an advisory decision divorced from an administrable record. Given those threshold defects, I would vote to affirm/deny relief on vehicle and preservation grounds rather than reach the merits.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal civilian employee who is a military reservist ordered to active duty under 10 U.S.C. § 12301(d) during a national emergency is entitled to “reservist differential pay” under 5 U.S.C. § 5538 because that service is “under a provision of law referred to in” 10 U.S.C. § 101(a)(13)(B).
case_analysis.legal_provision: 5 U.S.C. § 5538 (reservist differential pay), incorporating 10 U.S.C. § 101(a)(13)(B) (definition cross-reference to provisions of law for “contingency operation”), with 10 U.S.C. § 12301(d) (voluntary active-duty orders with member consent) as the activation authority at issue.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues the Federal Circuit’s interpretation contradicts the statutory text: because § 101(a)(13)(B) covers service “under a provision of law … during a national emergency,” any reservist called to active duty under § 12301(d) while a national emergency is ongoing has necessarily been ordered under a qualifying “provision of law” during a national emergency, triggering § 5538 differential pay; alternatively, petitioner emphasizes that his activation orders expressly invoked an emergency declaration, which should satisfy any required nexus to the emergency.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (DOT/United States) argues that § 5538 does not extend differential pay to all § 12301(d) voluntary activations merely because a national emergency exists; instead, the statutory cross-reference requires a tighter connection—i.e., the activation must be tied to/authorized by emergency- or contingency-related authorities covered by § 101(a)(13)(B), and § 12301(d) (standing, consent-based authority) does not qualify on that theory; the government also contends the case is a poor vehicle because petitioner did not properly raise certain factual/legal arguments below and did not follow agency procedures to request/pay-calculate the differential pay (e.g., submitting orders and leave/earnings statements).
key_precedents: Adams (referenced as controlling/relevant authority in the government’s brief; full citation not provided in the excerpts)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s Germain-based textual argument presses hardest: the residual clause says “any other provision of law during … a national emergency,” and “during” can read temporally. But, as Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett explain, § 5538 does not incorporate a time condition; it incorporates “a provision of law referred to in” § 101(a)(13)(B), and reading the catchall as a free-floating temporal trigger would largely nullify that provision-by-provision limitation and create sweeping payroll consequences without a clear statement. Justice Thomas’s vehicle point under United States v. Williams further counsels minimalism: we should not decide the unpreserved “orders expressly invoked the emergency” theory or announce any broad rule on an underdeveloped record. A narrow affirmance—§ 5538 does not reach § 12301(d) activations absent a meaningful connection to the declared emergency, and we do not reach alternative theories—best preserves statutory structure and institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best argument is that § 101(a)(13)(B)’s residual clause says “any other provision of law during … a national emergency,” and that the word “during” suggests a purely temporal trigger. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, § 5538 does not incorporate a time period; it incorporates, provision-by-provision, “a provision of law referred to in” § 101(a)(13)(B), and that cross-reference cannot be read to erase Congress’s choice to tie eligibility to the legal authority under which the member is ordered rather than to the mere existence of an emergency. I also agree with Justice Gorsuch (and the Chief Justice) that United States v. Williams counsels restraint here: petitioner’s “orders expressly invoked the emergency” theory was not pressed or passed upon below, and we should not expand the statutory question on this vehicle. Under an original public meaning reading, § 12301(d)’s standing, consent-based authority is not transformed into an emergency-conditioned provision simply because an emergency happens to be ongoing.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is the surface text of § 101(a)(13)(B)’s residual clause—“any other provision of law during … a national emergency”—which, read in isolation, could be purely temporal. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 5538(a) does not ask whether service occurred during an emergency; it incorporates a category of “provision[s] of law referred to in” § 101(a)(13)(B), so reading “during” to convert § 12301(d) into a covered provision whenever any emergency exists would largely nullify the incorporation’s limiting function and create an expansive wage entitlement Congress did not clearly express. Justice Thomas’s and Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on United States v. Williams further supports restraint: petitioner’s alternative “orders expressly invoked the emergency” theory was not pressed or passed upon below, making this a poor vehicle to announce a broad temporal-trigger rule. On a textualist reading attentive to structure and practical consequences, § 12301(d)’s standing, consent-based authority is not an emergency-referred provision merely because an emergency declaration is contemporaneously in effect.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s structural/surplusage concern seriously: a purely time-based reading could make § 5538 eligibility depend on long-running emergency declarations in a way Congress may not have anticipated. But the enacted residual clause in § 101(a)(13)(B)—“any other provision of law during … a national emergency”—is exactly the sort of broad, protective catchall Congress uses in remedial schemes, and I do not think we may rewrite “during” to mean “during and because of” absent textual support, especially where that narrowing falls hardest on financially vulnerable reservists. Justice Thomas’s and Justice Gorsuch’s Williams vehicle objection cuts against reaching petitioner’s alternative “orders expressly invoked the emergency” theory, but it does not justify adopting a narrowing nexus requirement as a matter of statutory meaning; at most it supports a limited remand or case-specific disposition without foreclosing § 12301(d) categorically. On my pragmatic reading, Congress chose breadth to ensure access to make-whole pay protections in emergency periods, and administrability concerns cannot override the text when agencies can demand reasonable documentation rather than deny coverage wholesale.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best argument is the plain-language pull of the residual clause—“any other provision of law during … a national emergency”—and her Germain point that we should not add words like “because of.” But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett stress, § 5538 does not incorporate a freestanding temporal condition; it incorporates “a provision of law referred to in” § 101(a)(13)(B), and reading “during” to cover any standing authority used while an emergency happens to persist makes that provision-focused cross-reference largely surplus and administratively unmoored. I also find Justice Thomas’s Williams vehicle concern reinforcing: petitioner’s “express invocation in the orders” theory and the missing agency predicate mean this record is a poor platform to announce a broad, time-based entitlement rule. Under my pragmatic textualism, the more coherent reading requires some meaningful linkage between the activation authority and the emergency—not mere simultaneity—and petitioner hasn’t cleanly established that here.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that the residual clause’s words—“any other provision of law during … a national emergency”—have surface breadth, and Germain cautions us not to add limitations the text does not contain. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan explain, § 5538 does not incorporate a time period; it incorporates “a provision of law referred to in” § 101(a)(13)(B), and reading “during” as a freestanding temporal trigger would largely nullify the provision-focused cross-reference and erase Congress’s line-drawing among activation authorities. In context—§ 101(a)(13)(B) defining “contingency operation”—the better textual reading is that the catchall captures other emergency-occasioned call-up provisions, not standing, consent-based authorities like § 12301(d) merely used while an emergency exists. I also agree with Justice Roberts’s and Justice Thomas’s Williams-based vehicle concern: petitioner’s “orders expressly invoked the emergency” theory was not pressed or passed upon below, so we should not use this case to announce a broader rule on an underdeveloped record.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s textual argument, invoking Germain, is the petitioner’s best point: the residual clause’s phrase “any other provision of law during … a national emergency” has a plausible temporal reading. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, § 5538 incorporates a category of “provision[s] of law referred to in” § 101(a)(13)(B), and reading “during” as purely coincidental effectively collapses that provision-focused limitation into an open-ended wage entitlement whenever an emergency declaration happens to be in force—an administratively unstable expansion Congress did not clearly enact. I also agree with the Roberts/Thomas vehicle concern under United States v. Williams that petitioner’s alternative “orders expressly invoked the emergency” theory was not pressed or passed upon below, counseling institutional restraint and a narrow affirmance on this record. Accordingly, I would affirm that § 12301(d) voluntary activations are not covered absent a meaningful connection to the declared emergency, and I would not reach unpreserved theories about the orders’ language.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—invoking Germain—is that the residual clause in § 101(a)(13)(B) says “any other provision of law during … a national emergency,” and on its face “during” can be read temporally. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 5538(a) does not incorporate a free-floating time condition; it incorporates “a provision of law referred to in” § 101(a)(13)(B), and a purely temporal reading would largely nullify that provision-by-provision limitation and render the rest of the enumerated contingency authorities surplusage. I also agree with Justice Gorsuch and Justice Thomas that Williams counsels restraint here: the alternative “express invocation in the orders” theory was not pressed or passed upon below, so this is a poor vehicle to expand the statute beyond what the cross-reference, read in context, naturally bears. On an original public meaning and structural reading, § 12301(d) remains a standing, consent-based authority and is not transformed into an emergency-referred provision merely because an emergency exists in the background.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s Germain-based argument presses the best textual point—“during” can read as purely temporal—but it underestimates how § 5538’s phrase “under a provision of law referred to in” makes the cross-reference operate provision-by-provision, not as an all-purpose time switch. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, a purely temporal reading would largely erase the limiting function of Congress’s incorporation and turn § 5538 into an open-ended wage entitlement whenever an emergency declaration persists, a practical consequence that cuts against a sensible, administrable line-drawing in a payroll statute. I also find the Williams vehicle concern, flagged by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas, important under my pragmatic approach: the “orders expressly invoked the emergency” theory and the record gaps make this a poor case to announce the broader rule petitioner seeks. Those points together leave me persuaded that some meaningful connection between the authority used and the emergency is required, and that § 12301(d) standing, consent-based orders do not qualify on these facts.

John Roberts.reasoning: Given my commitment to narrow rulings and institutional legitimacy, I would not extend 5 U.S.C. § 5538 to all voluntary activations under 10 U.S.C. § 12301(d) merely because a national emergency exists; the cross-reference to 10 U.S.C. § 101(a)(13)(B) is best read to require a meaningful nexus between the call to active duty and the emergency/contingency operation, rather than treating the mere temporal overlap as sufficient. The government’s vehicle objections reinforce restraint: key arguments about whether an express invocation of an emergency declaration in the orders suffices were “not pressed or passed upon” below, counseling against resolving that broader issue here. See United States v. Williams, 504 U.S. 36, 41 (1992). On these grounds, I would affirm without announcing an expansive interpretation that could disrupt settled administrative practice and federal payroll obligations.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 5 U.S.C. § 5538 extends differential pay only when the employee’s active duty is “under a call or order to active duty under a provision of law referred to in” 10 U.S.C. § 101(a)(13)(B), which in turn focuses on service ordered “during a national emergency declared by the President or Congress.” Reading that cross-reference to cover every voluntary activation under 10 U.S.C. § 12301(d) merely because an emergency exists would effectively erase Congress’s limiting choice to tie eligibility to the particular “provision of law” described in § 101(a)(13)(B), rather than to any activation contemporaneous with an emergency. Moreover, this case is a poor vehicle to decide any broader nexus question because petitioner did not press or preserve in the court of appeals the claim that his specific orders’ express emergency invocation sufficed—an issue “not pressed or passed upon” below. See United States v. Williams, 504 U.S. 36, 41 (1992).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of 5 U.S.C. § 5538(a) ties differential pay to active duty “under a provision of law referred to in” 10 U.S.C. § 101(a)(13)(B), and § 12301(d) is a standing, consent-based authority that does not itself depend on a war or emergency declaration. Reading the cross-reference to sweep in any voluntary § 12301(d) activation whenever any national emergency exists would effectively convert § 5538 into a broad wage guarantee untethered to contingency-related service, a substantial practical expansion Congress did not clearly enact. In addition, this is a poor vehicle because key arguments about an “express invocation” of an emergency declaration in the orders were not pressed or passed upon below, and petitioner did not follow agency procedures necessary to calculate any differential pay, counsels against disturbing the judgment. See United States v. Williams, 504 U.S. 36, 41 (1992).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 5538(a) grants reservist differential pay when an employee is ordered to active duty “under a provision of law referred to in” 10 U.S.C. § 101(a)(13)(B), and that cross-reference expressly includes “any other provision of law during … a national emergency declared by the President or Congress.” Read naturally, that language is satisfied by service ordered under 10 U.S.C. § 12301(d) so long as it occurs during a declared national emergency, without importing extra nexus requirements not found in the text. The government’s narrower construction effectively rewrites the statute by treating § 5538 as if it incorporated the full “contingency operation” concept rather than § 101(a)(13)(B)’s list, contrary to the Court’s instruction that courts must follow enacted text over free-floating legislative purpose, see Connecticut Nat’l Bank v. Germain, 503 U.S. 249, 253–54 (1992). Any remaining procedural or vehicle concerns about documentation go to administration of the benefit, not the threshold statutory entitlement for reservists serving during an emergency.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 5538(a) turns on whether the employee’s active-duty service was “under a provision of law referred to in” 10 U.S.C. § 101(a)(13)(B), and § 101(a)(13)(B)’s residual clause (“any other provision of law during a … national emergency”) is best read to require some nexus between the activating legal authority and the emergency, not merely temporal coincidence with an ongoing declaration. Treating 10 U.S.C. § 12301(d)—a standing, consent-based authority—as categorically triggering differential pay whenever any national emergency exists would expand § 5538 beyond a workable, administrable boundary and risk severing the cross-reference from the “contingency operation” concept Congress used to define the covered universe. In addition, this case presents substantial vehicle problems because the asserted “express invocation” theory was not “pressed or passed upon” below and the agency never had the required materials to calculate differential pay, a posture in which we typically decline to resolve the broader interpretive question. See United States v. Williams, 504 U.S. 36, 41 (1992).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The text of 5 U.S.C. § 5538 ties differential pay to service “under a provision of law referred to in” 10 U.S.C. § 101(a)(13)(B), which in turn describes orders “under a provision of law” during a national emergency; that cross-reference is best read to require that the member be ordered to active duty under an emergency-referenced statutory authority, not merely under § 12301(d)’s standing, consent-based activation power while an emergency happens to exist. Reading § 5538 to cover all § 12301(d) activations whenever any national emergency is ongoing would effectively erase the limiting function of the incorporated reference and expand the statute beyond its enacted terms, a result inconsistent with ordinary textual limits on incorporations by reference. And even if petitioner’s alternative “orders expressly invoked the emergency” theory might matter, it was not “pressed or passed upon” below, making this a poor vehicle for resolving that question under United States v. Williams, 504 U.S. 36, 41 (1992).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 5538(a) ties differential pay to service “pursuant to a call or order to active duty under a provision of law referred to in” § 101(a)(13)(B), and the more workable reading—consistent with history and the statute’s structure—is that the referenced “any other provision of law … during a national emergency” requires a meaningful nexus between the activation authority and the emergency, not mere coincidence with an extant emergency declaration while using the standing, consent-based authority in 10 U.S.C. § 12301(d). Extending § 5538 to all § 12301(d) activations whenever a national emergency exists would sweep broadly and unpredictably, raising practical administration and line-drawing concerns that Congress likely would have addressed more directly. In addition, this is a poor vehicle because key arguments about the content of the orders and the emergency nexus were not “pressed or passed upon” below and petitioner did not follow agency procedures to request/calculate the differential, counseling restraint. Under United States v. Williams, we generally decline to decide important questions on an underdeveloped record and issues not properly presented in the court of appeals.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 5538(a) ties entitlement to differential pay to the employee’s “call or order to active duty” being issued “under * * * a provision of law referred to in” 10 U.S.C. § 101(a)(13)(B), which in turn points to activation authorities used for contingency operations, not any standing authority that happens to be used while an emergency exists. Reading § 101(a)(13)(B)’s catchall (“any other provision of law during * * * a national emergency”) to sweep in § 12301(d) would make differential pay turn on the happenstance of an emergency’s pendency, collapsing the statute’s provision-focused cross-reference into an unlimited temporal rule and creating significant surplusage against the more specific emergency-related activation provisions already enumerated. The better textual reading—consistent with methodological discipline in cross-references—is that “during a national emergency” requires the activation authority to be one invoked because of (i.e., in connection with) the emergency, rather than merely contemporaneous with it; the Federal Circuit’s approach in Adams supports that narrower construction. Because § 12301(d) is a consent-based, generally available authority not itself keyed to emergency declarations, petitioner’s orders are not “under” a qualifying provision as § 5538 uses that term.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 5538 grants differential pay only when the employee is called to active duty “under a provision of law referred to in” 10 U.S.C. § 101(a)(13)(B), and the better reading—given that § 101(a)(13)(B) defines “contingency operation”—is that the call-up must be substantively tied to the war or national-emergency authorization, not merely contemporaneous with an emergency. Treating any § 12301(d) voluntary activation as qualifying whenever an emergency exists would collapse the cross-reference and render Congress’s triggering limitation largely superfluous, contrary to ordinary structural canons reflected in this Court’s statutory approach. Separately, this case is an especially poor vehicle because key arguments about the content of petitioner’s orders and any emergency nexus were not “pressed or passed upon” below, and the record indicates petitioner did not follow agency procedures necessary to request/calculate the differential pay. United States v. Williams, 504 U.S. 36, 41 (1992).
